title: Charles I (Oxford) to Prince Rupert, 29 April 1645, BL Add MS 18983 f. 14 (DECODE R4921)

transcription.source: DECODE image IMG_R4921_I28579_P1, read in crops
transcription.notes: Holograph, marked 'Duplicate'. Clear opening and close with cipher runs between clear words; ciphertext.txt is transcription.txt with the clear words removed. 30 Sept 2026: the sign first transcribed as group e5 in 'come e5 fetch' is the King's clear '&' (its form matches the clear '&' of the opening and subscription, not his e5 groups), so ciphertext.txt has 304 groups, not 305.

system.summary: Homophonic alphabet on numbers 1-80 with a nomenclator of letter+digit groups and 3-digit numbers, plus 81-98 as nulls or rare codes: the key Lasry reconstructed as TNA SP106-5.
system.notes: Groups 81-98 are outside the key. 95 (my) and 98 (artillery) read from context; the rest sit at phrase ends.

prior_solution.where: No decipherment of this letter found (Warburton 1849, Bromley 1787, web). The key is Lasry's 2020 DECODE reconstruction for other letters (R929).

conditions.human_role: Project-level: obtained a DECODE login with privileges and passed its session cookie (from the browser developer tools) to the model, set up Claude Code with Fable 5.1 or Opus 5, and posed the problem with /goal. No target-specific intervention recorded.

solution.what: Fetched the R4921 images and the sibling records R4916-R4922, keys R8627, R8724, R9116 with the shared DECODE cookie.
Warburton, Memoirs of Prince Rupert vol. 3 (1849): Digby 27 and 30 April 1645 printed, this letter not. Bromley 1787 and a web search: nothing.
Transcribed the 305 cipher groups from crops of the page image.
Ciphertext-only homophonic anneal on the numeric groups (code groups as gaps), 4 restarts with the en-1640s model: no agreement between runs.
Tested the Duke of Richmond cipher of R4922 (31 July 1645, interlined): its letter values run past 100, ours stop at 98.
Checked the Digby-Walsingham key R8724 and Digby's cipher list R8627: a different system.
R9116, a period tally of a King-to-Queen cipher (Oxford 1642), uses the same letter+digit groups, pointing to the King-Queen cipher family.
Applied Lasry's reconstructed key TNA SP106-5 (DECODE R929) unchanged: fluent English at once (FOR THE PRESENT ... TO TRANSPORT ... SENT FOR GORING ... NO TIME SHALL BE LOST).
Read 95 = my and 98 = artillery from context; c2 = do, b2 = can, k4 = nor, 412ant = warrant as conjectures; about 15 code groups left open.
Content matches Digby's letters of 27 and 30 April 1645 (the King cannot bring the train to Rupert; Rupert should march) and Rupert's march on Oxford in May.

Correction after an outside check of the phrase 'you may come and fetch it' against the key: the groups 68 4 | 75 86 93 c-o-m-e e5 f-e-t-c-h 83 f2 give y-e-u [86][93] come IN fetch it. On the image the 4 stands at the torn edge (probably 45, so 'you'); 86 and 93 are outside the key and mark phrase ends elsewhere, so 'may' is supplied, not read; and the sign transcribed e5 is the King's clear '&' (same form as in 'friday & sonday' and 'Oncle & most', unlike his three small e5 groups), so 'and' stands as his own word. Transcription and ciphertext corrected (304 groups); page, reading.md and NOTES now print 'you [may] come and fetch it'.

outcome.method: read after matching with key from external sources
outcome.method_basis: Lasry's King-Queen key 'TNA SP106-5' on DECODE R929 (SP 106/10, a different collection) was found to fit after a frequency-tally record (R9116) pointed to that family, and read the letter unchanged.
outcome.fraction_read_source: ciphertext.txt: 304 groups (305 until the 30 Sept 2026 correction); 15 unread = code groups with no key value, read only from context (61, 211, 186, 214, 376, 148, 412, 327, c1, d4, e4 x2, o1, 03, 05); the 30 tokens of groups 81-98 other than 95/98 counted read as nulls/stops (if counted unread: 0.85); 95=my, 98=artillery counted read
outcome.notes: Read with Lasry's SP106-5 key. The sense is complete; about 20 of 304 groups (code words) are open or read from context only.
